newsitem.title: USA: FBI issues new plea for Olympic bombing information.
newsitem.headline: FBI issues new plea for Olympic bombing information.

text.p: The explosion that rocked a crowded Centennial Olympic Park last summer, injuring more than 100 people and killing two people, may have been the largest pipe bomb ever detonated in this country, officials said Wednesday.
The FBI renewed its appeal for the public's help in solving the case and said it has identified about a hundred people who were near the site of the July 27 explosion.
The agency said it has determined, within 20 minutes, when a green, military-style knapsack containing the bomb was placed in the park.
David Johnson, the special agent in charge of the FBI's Atlanta office, said the pipe bomb that went off on July 27 was "enormous" and "possibly the largest ever detonated in this country."

A toll-free number (1-888-324-8404) was set up Wednesday to allow people to hear the warning call that was made to a 911 emergency number from a pay telephone 22 minutes before the blast occurred. The recording of the brief call was made public by the agency in December.
"We're trying to generate more leads," said FBI spokesman Jay Spadafore. He said the toll-free number would operate during the next 30 days.

The FBI said a 100-member task force examined and catalogued more than 5,000 photographs received since the agency asked for the public's help on Dec. 9, when a $500,000 reward was offered for information leading to an arrest and conviction in the case.
Investigators have also conducted a frame-by-frame analysis of hundreds of videotapes that have been received, the agency said.
"Both the videotapes and photographs have been very useful to us in narrowing the window during which the bomb was planted," Spadafore said.

He would not identify the 20-minute period during which investigators believe the bomb was placed in front of the tower. The FBI said in December that the knapsack containing the pipe bomb was placed under a bench near a sound and light tower between midnight and 12:45 a.m.
"There are many encouraging aspects of the investigation, including the forensic analysis," Johnson said. "We have made and continue to make substantial progress on the investigation."
Security guard Richard Jewell was initially named a suspect in the investigation, but was cleared by authorities in October.
